The ethics question is the one candidates prepare least, and it shows. When I ask for an ethical dilemma, most people describe something that was never a dilemma. Somebody offered them money, and they said no. That is not a dilemma. That is the law. A dilemma is when two things you believe in point in different directions, and you have to choose. The client needs the building on time, and your engineer tells you the schedule is not safe. What I want to hear is how you thought about it. Which rule did you have to follow, which one did you choose to follow, and what did it cost you? And one more thing. You do not have to be the hero of the story. Some of the best answers I have heard end with the candidate admitting that he bent a rule once, and explaining exactly why he would not do it again.

A supplier invited me to his beach house for a long weekend, with my family, and he was very clear that he wanted nothing in return. We were in the middle of choosing the steel supplier for our biggest project, and his company was one of three on the list. There was no rule against it, not in writing. Our code said we must not accept gifts, and a weekend is not exactly a gift. So I did what I now tell every engineer to do. I asked myself whether I would be comfortable if the story were in the newspaper the next day. I was not. I declined politely, and I disclosed the invitation to my uncle the same afternoon. We added one line to the code that month: any invitation from a supplier has to be reported, whatever it is. His company won the contract anyway, three weeks later, on price. Nobody had to wonder why.
